scenes.vo: There are only four things the State needs to convict an innocent man. In 1997, South Carolina used all four on me.
Rule one: you don't need evidence. You need a story, told with a straight face.
scenes.onscreen:
You don't need evidence.
You need a story, told
with a straight face.

scenes.vo: Rule two: a jury that trusts the badge more than the facts.
scenes.onscreen:
A jury that trusts the
badge more than the facts.

scenes.vo: Rule three: a record nobody actually reads.
Rule four: time. The longer they hold you, the more people assume you belong there.

scenes.vo: Three years and eleven months later, every judge on the South Carolina Supreme Court said the same thing: it should have been impossible to convict me. Unanimous. Then they withdrew the opinion, refiled it, and deleted the words — while the State was still holding me past the order.
scenes.onscreen:
State v. Martin
Op. No. 25093
March 27, 2000
→ refiled June 12, 2000

scenes.vo: My lawyer, Dan Stacey, gave me one instruction before he died: get those words into a record nobody can edit.
This is that record. Clearly Established. Link in bio. Comment which rule you've watched them use.
